profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Oregon State Data Center in Salem, the state capital, operated by Enterprise Information Services, the state central IT agency, under its Data Center Services program, providing centralized data center hosting for Oregon state agencies. This facility is unrelated to a separate, much larger private data center campus proposed for the Salem area by a company called Verrus, a 5.1 billion dollar commercial project for which Oregon's governor directed the withdrawal of state owned land in 2026 amid public opposition; that project is a distinct commercial entity and should not be conflated with this state government facility. No detailed capacity or megawattage figures for this facility were published on the state's own site as of this research. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
The Oregon State Data Center in Salem is a government facility operated by the state's central IT agency to host systems for Oregon state agencies. No capacity or power figures are published by the operator, so its size relative to Oregon's other data center infrastructure cannot be determined from official sources. The state has mapped 133 data centers across Oregon, of which only 8 have published megawatt figures totaling 156.6 MW.

Without published specifications, this facility does not rank among Oregon's disclosed capacity, though it is catalogued as a mapped site. The 8 facilities with published power in the state represent the only infrastructure for which scaling decisions can be assessed. A state government data center typically runs at lower density than commercial AI training operations and serves agency workloads rather than frontier compute, making it structurally distinct from the facilities that constrain large-scale AI development.

This site has no bearing on whether the power grid is the binding constraint on AI scaling in Oregon. To evaluate that question requires the published capacity figures of commercial operators, which exist for only a small fraction of the state's mapped infrastructure. The absence of published data from this facility means it does not factor into assessments of available capacity for AI compute.
